method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)' (first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030), 20 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0. eviQ also states that its content should not be hosted on external sites, and that commercial entities must contact eviQ to seek permission (https://www.eviq.org.au/copyright). Adaptations must cite the eviQ ID, version and URL. (read at https://www.eviq.org.au/copyright (Disclaimer and copyright page)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621) 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)' (published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue)), 8 claims; LICENCE: © Endocrine Society. All rights reserved (read at endocrine.org site footer and https://www.endocrine.org/terms-of-use). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim and anchor (S1, eviQ 486) unchanged and adds S2, the Endocrine Society 2023 GRADE guideline, read from the society's own guideline page (its essential points and all eight recommendations). The full JCEM article was behind a bot challenge, so S2's rationale, doses and evidence tables were not read.

claims.claim: **Hypercalcaemia of malignancy means an albumin-corrected calcium above 2.6 mmol/L**, or above the laboratory's upper reference limit, in a person with cancer.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No formal severity scale exists, but a common split is:** mild 2.6 to under 3.1 mmol/L, moderate 3.1 to 3.4 mmol/L, severe above 3.4 mmol/L.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start treatment for anyone with symptoms or a calcium above 3.1 mmol/L.** Severe hypercalcaemia is a medical emergency and is treated aggressively.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Up to 30 percent of people with cancer develop it, and it carries a poor prognosis.** Breast and renal cancer, myeloma, lymphoma and squamous cell cancers are the usual causes, mostly through a tumour protein that behaves like parathyroid hormone.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Three main mechanisms drive bone calcium release:** lytic bone metastases releasing cytokines (typical of myeloma); tumour PTH-related protein, which also makes the kidney hold calcium (breast, head and neck, kidney and lung squamous cancers); and tumour-made calcitriol, which also boosts gut absorption (some lymphomas).
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Primary hyperparathyroidism is common and can coexist with cancer;** a PTH level tells them apart.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptoms are often vague and can look like advanced cancer or treatment side effects:** thirst, polyuria, confusion, weakness, fatigue, anorexia and constipation; when severe, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy and a falling conscious level, which can progress to coma and death. Arrhythmias are uncommon. How fast the calcium rose matters as well as the level.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Grade 3 (above 3.1 to 3.4 mmol/L)** may be tolerated if it rose slowly, but a rapid rise causes marked symptoms and usually needs prompt treatment. **Grade 4 (above 3.4 mmol/L) needs urgent correction regardless of symptoms**, because of the risk of arrhythmia and coma.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Correct calcium for albumin:** corrected calcium (mmol/L) = measured calcium (mmol/L) + 0.02 × (40 − albumin in g/L).
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Also check** creatinine, electrolytes with phosphate and magnesium, PTH (for primary hyperparathyroidism), PTHrP (for humoral hypercalcaemia), 1,25- and 25-hydroxy vitamin D, TSH and vitamin A, plus an ECG for a short QT or other conduction changes.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Goals: relieve symptoms, return corrected calcium to normal and, where possible, treat the cancer.** Stop or cut back medicines that raise calcium, such as thiazides, calcitriol, calcium supplements, antacids and lithium.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Symptomatic hypercalcaemia generally needs prompt, often inpatient, care with IV fluids and a bisphosphonate.**
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rehydration is essential:** these patients are dry, and a low GFR further blocks calcium excretion. Give IV sodium chloride 0.9%, tailored to volume, cardiac and renal status; for acute severe hypercalcaemia in an adult, 4 to 6 litres over 24 hours is a reasonable rate.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Watch for fluid overload in older patients or with renal impairment.** Loop diuretics do not lower calcium and are used only for fluid overload, with potassium and phosphate monitored and replaced. Calcium reaches its lowest point at 2 to 4 days; severe renal failure may need dialysis.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate) work fast and durably.** Local policy may decide which; zoledronic acid is often preferred as it is more potent and infuses in 15 minutes against 2 hours for pamidronate.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Bisphosphonates are nephrotoxic:** good hydration helps protect the kidneys, and renal impairment may mean a dose change or avoiding them (see the product information). They can cause hypocalcaemia when vitamin D is deficient or PTH is suppressed.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Expect calcium to fall within 3 to 4 days, bottom out at 4 to 7 days, and stay down for 2 to 4 weeks.** Pamidronate can be repeated if calcium has not dropped within 48 hours; zoledronic acid can be repeated no sooner than 7 days for refractory or relapsed hypercalcaemia.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Denosumab (anti-RANKL) is an option if hypercalcaemia resists zoledronic acid, or bisphosphonates are ruled out by severe renal impairment.** It acts in about 4 days with a nadir by day 10. Hypocalcaemia is a real risk, especially with poor kidney function, so monitor calcium regularly.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Calcitonin works within hours, but tolerance sets in within 48 to 72 hours.** It is most useful, with fluids and a bisphosphonate, for symptomatic severe hypercalcaemia (calcium above 3.5 mmol/L): calcitonin gives the quick drop, the bisphosphonate the lasting one. No renal dose change is needed; the Australian product is calcitonin salmon (salcatonin).
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Glucocorticoids are the primary treatment when excess gut calcium absorption is the cause** (vitamin D toxicity, granulomatous disease, some lymphomas). They take roughly 2-4 days to work; taper them off to avoid adrenal insufficiency.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, '486 Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HCM) (eviQ ID 486, version 5)', first approved 1 July 2005; last reviewed 26 June 2026; review due 30 June 2030, https://www.eviq.org.au/p/486, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **HCM is the commonest metabolic complication of cancer, with high morbidity and mortality.** S2's aims are to control the calcium and to stop it coming back.
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat every adult with HCM with denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate** rather than without either (recommendation; very low certainty).
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2 suggests denosumab in preference to an IV bisphosphonate** (conditional; very low certainty), a different first choice from S1.
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe HCM (calcium above 3.5 mmol/L): start calcitonin together with the bisphosphonate or denosumab,** and stop calcitonin after 48–72 hours because it loses effect (conditional). This matches S1.
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Refractory or recurrent HCM despite an IV bisphosphonate: add denosumab** (conditional).
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Calcitriol-driven HCM (for example lymphoma): glucocorticoids first;** add an IV bisphosphonate or denosumab if calcium stays severe or symptomatic despite them (conditional).
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Hypercalcaemia from parathyroid carcinoma: a calcimimetic, an IV bisphosphonate or denosumab** (conditional). With mild hypercalcaemia and symptoms, start the calcimimetic; with moderate to severe hypercalcaemia, start the bisphosphonate or denosumab, which act faster and are better tolerated than rising calcimimetic doses.
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **If one approach does not control it, add the other** (a bisphosphonate or denosumab to a calcimimetic, or a calcimimetic to them). Consider surgery once severe hypercalcaemia is controlled.
claims.locator: Endocrine Society (co-sponsored by the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research and the European Society of Endocrinology); El-Hajj Fuleihan G, Clines GA, Hu MI, et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 108(3):507 (doi 10.1210/clinem/dgac621), 'Treatment of Hypercalcemia of Malignancy in Adults: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (essential points and list of recommendations)', published online 21 December 2022 (March 2023 issue), https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/hypercalcemia, retrieved 2026-09-24
